entry.title: Testart v Testart (No 3) [2026] FCA 1558
entry.content:
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.

Key holding: A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

entry.title: Elizabeth Mitkovski v Certis Security Australia [2026] FWC 4115
entry.content:
Ms Mitkovski, a part-time Aviation Screening Officer at Sydney Airport, sought flexible working arrangements to accommodate her caring responsibilities and disputed Certis Security Australia’s refusals of two requests. The Fair Work Commission considered whether Certis had discussed and genuinely tried to reach agreement, had regard to the consequences of refusal, and refused on reasonable business grounds under s 65A(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).

Key holding: A refusal of a flexible working arrangement request is supported by reasonable business grounds where the employer’s reasons are rational and sound and related to its operational requirements and obligations.

I find that the reasons relied upon by Certis constitute reasonable business grounds for the refusal of the requests. Each reason is rational and sound, and related to the Respondent's operational requirements and obligations.

entry.title: Mr Johnathon Burr v The Trustee for Cornerstone Labour Hire Unit Trust [2026] FWC 4121
entry.content:
Mr Burr’s host assignment with CEVA Logistics ended and he brought an unfair dismissal application against his labour-hire employer, Cornerstone. The Commission had to decide whether Cornerstone dismissed him or whether only his host placement ended; because Cornerstone kept him on its books and sought alternative work, the application was dismissed.

Key holding: Where a labour-hire employee’s host placement ends but the labour-hire employer remains ready and actively attempts to redeploy the employee, the employment has not been terminated on the employer’s initiative and there is no dismissal under s 386(1).

Under s 386(1), a person is considered dismissed if their employment with the employer has been terminated on the employer's initiative. It follows that if the employment continues or if the employer is actively seeking to find alternative work for the employee, there has been no dismissal.

entry.title: Madana Harrop v Maryborough District Health Service [2026] FWC 4112
entry.content:
Ms Harrop lodged an unfair dismissal application 16 days late after her union, the ANMF, failed to transmit a legal referral due to an automated email system error. The Fair Work Commission accepted representative error as a reasonable explanation, found exceptional circumstances and granted an extension of time. The merits of the unfair dismissal claim have not yet been determined.

Key holding: Where an applicant is blameless and reasonably relies on their representative, a delay caused by the representative’s administrative or system error can be an acceptable explanation for the whole delay and support a finding of exceptional circumstances under s 394(3).

In this case, the reason for the delay was the error of the ANMF, and it is in my view reasonable for the Applicant to have relied on the ANMF's advice that referral would have been made to her legal representatives to pursue an unfair dismissal application. The Applicant should not be disadvantaged because the ANMF experienced a system error in processing of the legal referral.

entry.title: Stephanie Tranquille v New Beginnings Network [2026] FWC 4113
entry.content:
This was an application by New Beginnings Network to vary an unfair dismissal compensation order so that it could pay $5,025 by instalments of $50 per week, citing financial hardship. The Fair Work Commission refused the amount sought but varied the order to allow 10 weekly instalments of $502.50, with superannuation payable on the original due date.

Key holding: Under s 393 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission has a broad discretion to permit unfair dismissal compensation to be paid by instalments, exercised by weighing the respondent’s business needs and likely compliance against the applicant’s need to access compensation within a reasonable period.

In McCarron, James v Commercial Facilities Management Pty Ltd T/A CFM Air Conditioning Pty Ltd [2013] FWC 3577 in ordering that compensation be paid in instalments Bissett C said that when considering the time period for the instalment payments to be made the business needs of the Respondent must be weighed against the needs of the Applicant to access the compensation.

entry.title: Yuanyuan (Denise) Wang v Hk Calibration Technologies Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3891
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined a s.365 application by Ms Yuanyuan (Denise) Wang against HK Calibration Technologies Pty Ltd. It upheld the employer’s jurisdictional objection, finding Ms Wang resigned but was not “dismissed” under s.386(1)(b) of the Fair Work Act 2009 because the employer’s conduct was not intended to end employment and did not leave her with no effective or real choice but to resign. The application was dismissed.

Key holding: For a resignation to be a dismissal under s.386(1)(b), the employer’s conduct must be intended to bring employment to an end or make resignation the probable result, leaving the employee no effective or real choice but to resign.

The test to be applied here is whether the employer engaged in the conduct with the intention of bringing the employment to an end or whether termination of the employment was the probably result of the employer's conduct such that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

entry.title: Communications, Electrical, Electronic, Energy, Information, Postal, Plumbing and Allied Services Union of Australia (128V) v Ausgrid [2026] FWC 4082
entry.content:
The ETU brought a s 739 dispute against Ausgrid over whether Leading Hands performing Emergency Response Coordinator (ERC) on-call duties in Newcastle/Lower Hunter should be paid higher duties at Level 1 of the D2 Field Supervisor band. The Commission found ERC work overlapped with the Leading Hand role and was not the work of a higher-band Field Supervisor, so clause 13 did not apply. It declined to dismiss for want of a live dispute but answered the formulated question “no”.

Key holding: A Leading Hand performing ERC duties is not entitled to higher duties pay under clause 13 because ERC work overlaps with and is contemplated by the Leading Hand role rather than being the responsibilities and duties of a higher-band Field Supervisor Role.

For the reasons set out above, I am not persuaded that the work performed by an ERC is to be regarded as that of a Field Supervisor and not that of a Leading Hand. Rather, I accept Mr Richardson's evidence that there is an overlap between the Roles when it comes to emergency response, and that such overlap is a feature of the R&P Framework.

entry.title: Mr Gabriel Roccisano v Chop Shop Post Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4091
entry.content:
Mr Roccisano applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy after being notified of his dismissal by Chop Shop Post Pty Ltd on 4 November 2025. His application, filed on 12 December 2025, was out of time on either possible calculation of the end date. Deputy President Butler refused to extend time, finding that the medical evidence did not establish incapacity to lodge and that distress, financial pressure and ignorance of the 21-day limit were not exceptional circumstances.

Key holding: For the purposes of s 394(3), the distress inherent in losing a job is not of itself an exceptional circumstance, and neither is an asserted psychological condition exceptional unless it is shown to have incapacitated the applicant from lodging within time.

As the cause of action is founded on something as inherently distressing as job loss, distress per se cannot be considered exceptional.

The employer did not object but asked that the extension be limited to 14 days because the unions had earlier agreed not to commence industrial action before 14 October 2026. Key holding: Under s.459(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Fair Work Commission has a discretion to extend the 30-day protected action period by up to 30 days, and there is no statutory presumption as to the length of any extension.

As the length of the extension, I accept that the Commission has a discretion to grant a period up to 30 days. There is also no presumption about that length in the Act.

entry.title: Ms Vikki Turner v Ithaca Crystals Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4080
entry.content:
Ms Turner lodged an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Her former employer asserted she was not protected because it was a small business and she had not completed the minimum employment period. Ms Turner sought to amend to a general protections claim under s 586 (with an alternative extension of time under s 366(2)); the Commission held the application was in substance a general protections claim filed on the wrong form and allowed the amendment.

Key holding: Although s 586 cannot be used merely to substitute a general protections cause of action for an unfair dismissal claim so as to avoid ss 725/729, the Commission may waive the irregularity and permit amendment where the initiating application was in substance a general protections claim made on the wrong approved form.

Though there is no power to amend an application to substitute a general protections cause of action for an unfair dismissal one, that does not mean that the form in which the application is made is determinative. If a party simply uses the wrong form to make one type of claim or the other, that is an irregularity that can be corrected or waived pursuant to s 586 of the Fair Work Act: Hambridge v Spotless Facilities Services Pty Ltd

entry.title: Stephanie Tranquille v New Beginnings Network [2026] FWC 4103
entry.content:
New Beginnings Network sought that Commissioner Durham recuse herself from determining its s 603 application to vary a $5,025.00 compensation order made in favour of Ms Stephanie Tranquille, alleging apprehended bias arising from case management rulings, a conciliation conference and the Commissioner's conduct of the hearing. The Commissioner heard the recusal question herself on the papers and refused it. The substantive variation application remains outstanding, with the original compliance date of 22 October 2026 unaffected.

Key holding: A Commission member should not lightly accede to a recusal application, and apprehended bias is not established unless the applicant identifies the matter said to deflect the decision-maker from the merits and articulates the logical connection between that matter and the feared departure from impartial decision-making.

It is clear from the authorities to which I have referred that I should not lightly agree to recuse myself. New Beginnings have not provided substantial grounds to warrant me doing so.

entry.content:

The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application under s 399A after Mr Palmer repeatedly failed to comply with directions and to respond to the employer’s dismissal application. The merits and extension-of-time question were not determined.

Key holding: Under s 399A of the FW Act, the FWC may dismiss an application where an applicant unreasonably fails to comply with FWC directions, on the employer’s application and in the exercise of the FWC’s discretion.

entry.title: Application by United Workers' Union (108V) [2026] FWC 4066
entry.content:
The UWU applied for bargaining orders to stop a vote on a proposed Coles subsidiary enterprise agreement, alleging CNSCE had breached the good faith bargaining requirements. The Commission found a breach of s 228(1)(b) for failing to provide the draft agreement in time, but refused the orders because it was not reasonable in all the circumstances. Application dismissed.

Key holding: Timely disclosure of an available draft enterprise agreement is relevant information required by s 228(1)(b); however, a breach does not automatically justify a bargaining order because s 230 requires the Commission to be satisfied an order is reasonable in all the circumstances.

The failure to provide it represents a breach of the good faith bargaining obligations. However, for reasons which are explained below, including the UWU's own failure to present bargaining proposals, and failure to identify any issues it had adverted to with the proposed agreement after it received a copy of it ( on 8 October 2026), weigh against it being reasonable in all circumstances to make the orders sought.

entry.title: The Civil Air Operations Officers’ Association Of Australia Trading AS Civil Air v Airservices Australia [2026] FWC 3820
entry.content:
Civil Air applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to arbitrate a dispute about redundancy-type benefits under the Airservices Australia (Air Traffic Control and Supporting Air Traffic Services) Enterprise Agreement 2024-2027. The dispute concerned whether air traffic controllers who cannot obtain, or refuse to obtain, a National Security Clearance or Citizenship Eligibility Waiver are entitled to cl 62.13(a)(i)-(ii) benefits on termination.

Key holding: Clause 62.13 termination benefits require the employee to be a “potentially surplus employee” under cl 62.2, and inability or refusal to obtain an NSC or CEW does not make an ATC surplus where the class of ATCs remains required.

For these reasons I do not consider that employees who are unable or refuse to obtain an NSC (or CEW) can qualify for the entitlements in clause 62.13(a)(i) and (ii) because they are in a class of employees formally identified by the Respondent as a class which has a greater number of employees in it that is necessary for its efficient and economical working, within the meaning of clause 62.2(a) of the Agreement.

entry.title: Kacy Brazier v OS MCAP Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4043
entry.content:
This Fair Work Commission decision concerns an order for lost pay following an earlier finding that Kacy Brazier was unfairly dismissed and an order for his reinstatement. The Commission awarded reduced lost pay under s 391 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) because Brazier made no real attempt to find paid work for most of his unemployment and performed unpaid work for his then partner. Key holding: For a s.365 application at the material time, the Commission lacks jurisdiction unless the applicant was actually dismissed under s.386(1), meaning termination on the employer’s initiative or a resignation forced by employer conduct.

I have concluded that in this case there was no dismissal within the meaning of s.386 of the Act because I am satisfied there was no termination of the Applicant's employment on the Respondent's initiative and nor have I been persuaded that the Applicant was forced to resign because of conduct or a course of conduct engaged in by the Respondent .

He brought an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application, finding a valid reason and that the dismissal was not harsh, unjust or unreasonable.

Key holding: An employee’s failure to comply with a lawful and reasonable direction can constitute a valid reason for dismissal on the conduct ground.

A failure to follow a lawful and reasonable direction may give an employer a valid reason to dismiss an employee on the basis of their conduct.

entry.title: KCBC and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security second review) [2026] ARTA 2287
entry.content:
KCBC sought a second review of decisions rejecting claims for disability support pension (DSP), jobseeker payment (JSP) and special benefit. The Tribunal set aside the DSP rejection because it had been wrongly based on s 64 of the Social Security (Administration) Act 1999 (Cth), but affirmed the JSP and special benefit rejections.

Key holding: Where jobseeker payment is not payable due to the operation of s 64 of the Administration Act, special benefit is also not payable under s 729(4) of the Social Security Act.

The Tribunal accepted that, in circumstances where jobseeker payment was not payable due to the operation of section 64 of the Administration Act, special benefit would not be payable to the Applicant due to the operation of subsection 729(4) of the Social Security Act.
